text:
maria: Heads-up — after the autoscale spike this morning we saw a sustained drop in KV prefix hit-rate across the new replicas. Baseline cluster hit-rate ~78% -> post-scale 41-48% on newly spun nodes. p50 latency went 45ms -> 110ms, token cost ~2.1x. Anyone seen something similar?

jake: can you drop the grafana panels + query? want to correlate with batch sizes and kernel selection churn.

maria: grafana: https://grafana.internal/r/abc123 (top panel = prefix_hit_rate, bottom = p50_latency). Prom query I used: 
```
sum(rate(kv_prefix_hits_total[5m])) / sum(rate(kv_prefix_lookups_total[5m]))
```
Results show a sharp dip coincident with autoscaler scale-up at ~12:03.

ops-bot: Autoscaler event: scaled replicas 12 -> 22 at 2026-03-17T12:03:00Z (policy: cpu-based burst).

kai: My guess: cold replica effect + cache keying detail. We recently added instance_id into the cache_key for safer eviction sharding. That makes every new pod present an empty keyspace (no shared cache), so warmers are required. Did we intend instance-level salt?

maria: right — change was to avoid cross-tenant collision when running multi-tenant hosts. But for dedicated pools this is unnecessary. If instance_id is present, warmup must run per-instance which explodes work.

andre: proposal: two-part prewarm strategy: 1) deploy-time light warmers that hit the top N prefixes (by weight) per replica, rate limited. 2) asynchronous background backfill that continues warming low-frequency prefixes without blocking serving. Example prewarm curl: 
```
for key in $(cat top-prefixes.txt); do 
  curl -s -X POST $PREWARM_ENDPOINT -d "{\"prefix\":\"$key\"}" &
  sleep 0.05
done
```
This keeps SLO-friendly pacing.

maria: important concern: warmers themselves can cause SLO violations if they land during peak traffic. We need priority lanes and token bucket limits so prewarm requests have lower CPU priority and bounded qps.

perf-bot: quick profile summary from the regression run: cold-miss path dominates. Flame: ~60% time in kv_lookup_cold_miss -> disk/remote fetch path; 25% in model kernel warmup (cuda memmap), remainder in batching overhead. No obvious kernel regression.

jake: okay — that suggests warming KV entries matters most. Two follow-ups: 1) change cache_key to remove instance_id for dedicated pools only (config flag), 2) wire autoscaler lifecycle hooks to trigger prewarm jobs on scale-up.

kai: note on (1) — removing instance_id requires verifying tenant isolation still holds. Suggest switch to "pool_shard" key that maps many instances to same shard id, so cache is shared but still partitioned.

andre: about (2) k8s has no native pre-scale hook, but we can integrate with our autoscaler controller: when target_replicas increases, spawn a short-lived job that runs prewarm sampler against the new pods. Or use KEDA external scaler with scale notifications. Example CronJob-ish spec for timed warmers I mocked up: 
```
apiVersion: batch/v1
kind: Job
metadata: name: prewarm-on-scale
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: prewarmer
        image: redwood/prewarmer:canary
        env:
        - name: PREWARM_ENDPOINT
          value: "http://runtime-svc/prewarm"
      restartPolicy: Never
```
This job would run with a limited concurrency and inspect pod labels to distribute keys.

maria: also thinking about synthetic traffic: sample 5% of real incoming prefixes (weighted) and replay them against new replicas during ramp. That keeps warmers aligned to real workload distribution and avoids warming long-tail useless keys.

jake: good call. we should also hook into our batching heuristics: if new replicas report zero KV cache occupancy, temporarily favor smaller batches to reduce tail latencies until warm fraction reaches X%. Batching params: reduce max_batch_size from 32->12 for warmup window.

kai: hybrid strategy idea: shallow prefill (top 2k prefixes) synchronously on pod readiness, then async backfill for mid-tail, plus sticky routing that biases certain prefixes to warmed pods for a short period. That keeps hit-rate high without full warm of long-tail.

andre: here's a quick rate-limited prewarmer snippet that uses per-replica annotation to avoid double-warm: 
```
if [ -z "$(kubectl get pod $POD -o jsonpath='{.metadata.annotations.prewarmed}')" ]; then
  curl -X POST $PREWARM_ENDPOINT -d @top-prefixes.json
  kubectl annotate pod $POD prewarmed=true
fi
```
We should also add a TTL so pods re-warm after long idles.

maria: let's run an experiment: 10% of traffic routed to a canary pool with the new warmers + pool_shard keying + reduced batch size. Measure hit-rate, p50, and cost delta. I can run the traffic injection later today.

jake: I'll open an experiment branch and PR with the prewarmer container + controller hook. PR: https://git.internal/r/redwood/runtime-prewarm-experiment/PR-47

deploy-bot: rolled out canary image redwood/prewarmer:canary to cluster canary at commit abc123.

maria: thanks — I'll schedule the injection for 19:00 UTC and post a short checklist. If anyone wants to shadow metrics live ping me. :thumbsup:

jake: ack. I'll also add dashboards: prewarm_qps, per-replica cache_fill_pct, warmbacklog.

kai: if this works we should generalize warmers into the runtime's warm module and expose conservative defaults for Dedicated vs Hosted clusters.

andre: +1 to that. Also add an opt-in switch for aggressive per-instance warmers for workloads that need strict isolation.

maria: cool. action items: jake PR, andre job spec, kai keying changes, perf-bot run profile after canary. I'll coordinate the injection window.

jake: i'll create the dashboard and start the PR diff today.

maria: thanks team!
